Next month, the retail giant will allow you to use an AI agent on the site, with systems in place to let you approve and review purchases and set spending limits. The embrace of AI agents stands in stark contrast to Amazon, which blocked Perplexity's shopping agent and Meta's Muse AI assistant . But Walmart is opening its doors to AI shoppers - as long as they follow the retailer's rules. It has outlined a set of terms for agents, saying that "agents must not take actions beyond what the shopper intends" and cannot change a customer's payment method. items.title: What 32,000 Folds Did to the iPhone Duo's Hinge
items.snippet: Apple hasn't shared iPhone Duo hinge tests or given a lifetime fold number like Samsung, but Joanna Stern used a custom device to subject her review unit to more than 32,000 folds over four nights. Over the course of the testing, Stern said she thought it might be feeling looser as the number of folds increased, but her final conclusion was that she couldn't feel much of a change. A calibrated push-pull gauge used to take readings before and after the Duo fold test showed the hinge was actually stiffer than before. But in everyday use, I really couldn't feel a difference. items.title: iPhone Duo's Hidden FaceTime Camera Takes 'Trash' Photos
items.snippet: The iPhone Duo 's inner screen has an under-display front camera that's largely hidden from view. It's the first time we've seen an under-display camera on an iPhone, and it turns out there's a reason Apple hasn't used the technology before. Apple said the camera offers 1080p video recording, but didn't mention photo quality. items.title: Loop Capital Cuts Apple Rating Over iPhone Sales Outlook
items.snippet: Loop Capital has lowered its rating on Apple from "Buy" to "Hold," saying the company is unlikely to make up an estimated 13 million iPhone shipments cut from its plans for the second half of 2026, according to Investing.com . The firm reduced its Apple stock price target from $370 to $330. Loop previously believed shortages of memory and processors had delayed shipments that Apple would recover in 2027. Its latest supply chain checks have led it to drop that assumption. The firm now forecasts 79 million iPhone shipments in the December quarter, below initial estimates of 85 million. items.title: UK Proposes New Ways to Help Apple Pay Rivals
items.snippet: The UK's competition regulator has proposed changes to make it easier and cheaper for companies to offer alternatives to Apple Pay on the iPhone (via Reuters ). The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) says Apple's fees and restrictions make it too difficult for rivals to launch contactless payment apps. Its proposals would give developers more ways to access the iPhone's NFC technology, which allows users to pay by holding their device near a payment terminal. Apple opened up NFC access to developers in the UK in 2024, but companies must sign an agreement with Apple and pay fees. items.title: Today in Apple history: Macintosh PowerBook 100 makes laptops mainstream
items.snippet: October 21, 1991: Apple launches the Macintosh PowerBook 100 series. The lightweight Mac laptops will quickly become one of the most important tech gadgets of all time. These devices will almost single-handedly turn notebook computers into mainstream technology. Apple’s subsequent success in this category — whether it’s current MacBooks or even the rise of mobile devices like the iPhone — owes a huge debt to the PowerBook 100 series. Before the MacBook became the default laptop for creative professionals, Apple had to figure out how to make a computer genuinely portable. With the PowerBook 100, Apple didn’t just shrink the desktop Mac. It redefined what a computer could be when you took it out into the world. It established the laptop design we still recognize today, with a keyboard pushed back from the front edge and a pointing device nestled below it. That formula proved wildly successful, helping turn portable computing into a common experience. By modern standards, the PowerBook 100 series is the first true laptop Apple released. items.title: Netflix Lays Off 6 Percent of Staff
items.snippet: Joe Flint and Jessica Toonkel, reporting for The Wall Street Journal last week: Netflix is cutting 6% of its staff, or roughly 1,000 positions globally, its biggest round of layoffs since 2022, as it struggles with slowing growth and customer engagement. Co-Chief Executives Greg Peters and Ted Sarandos said in an email to employees Wednesday morning that the bulk of the cuts would be in the streaming giant’s product, tech, legal and human-resources teams. items.title: Time Magazine Profiles John Ternus
items.snippet: Andrew Chow, writing for Time: Just below the broad smile he’s been wearing all morning, John Ternus’ hands are shaking. On this September day in Silicon Valley, Apple’s new CEO is surrounded by celebrities, tech enthusiasts, and reporters who have flocked to Apple Park from around the world to catch a glimpse of the company’s new and long-awaited foldable phone, the Duo. After Ternus takes a few photos with the device, an Apple PR rep pulls the influencer known as IShowSpeed out of the crowd to meet him. items.snippet: The 4TB Samsung 990 Pro has its astronomical AI-driven high price slashed by 27%.

items.title: AMD brings official Ryzen overclocking to Linux with AOD driver support
items.snippet: New driver enablement work from AMD brings full platform-level tuning control to Ryzen systems running Linux, finally.

items.title: Qualcomm to cut jobs globally in "performance-based" layoffs, as company pivots to AI data center and edge computing markets
items.snippet: Qualcomm will begin performance-based layoffs worldwide in November as the chipmaker reallocates resources toward AI infrastructure, data centers, automotive, PCs, and edge computing, amid weaker consumer electronics demand.

items.title: FADU puts the filesystem inside the SSD's flash to bypass host CPUs
items.snippet: FADU’s FS-SSD carries NFSv3 file operations inside NVMe commands, letting GPUs, DPUs, and NICs read files without a host file system.

items.title: AMD and Intel will work together to create a single PyTorch code path for AI inference on CPUs
items.snippet: AMD and Intel are working together to bring CPU inference optimizations for PyTorch under the unified oneDNN library.

items.title: Samsung and SK Hynix are upgrading Chinese factories to produce advanced RAM chips as AI data center competition ramps up
items.snippet: Samsung and SK Hynix are reportedly upgrading their factories to produce more advanced RAM chips designed for AI data centers in an attempt to fend off competition from Chinese companies.

items.title: Why you don't need an audiophile headset for gaming — comfort, convenience, and a good mic win over pure audio fidelity
items.snippet: Headsets are mainly about audio, but that doesn't mean that the "objectively" best-sounding headset by audiophile standards translates to the best-sounding headset by gaming standards.

items.title: Micron's Taiwan union will launch a one-day strike this week, threatening memory production
items.snippet: Micron's Taiwan union is set to conduct a one-day strike at the company's Taoyuan DRAM facility as workers demand bonuses for this year and transparent terms of bonuses for upcoming years.

items.title: HPE says it will run the first supercomputer benchmarks on the Moon
items.snippet: HPE’s Spaceborne Computer-4 will ride Astrolab’s FLIP rover to the Moon’s south pole to run HPL, HPCG, and AI tests.

items.title: Jensen Huang Nvidia GTC keynote disrupted by Greenpeace protest over chips in Russian drones
items.snippet: Jensen Huang's Nvidia GTC keynote speech in Berlin was disrupted by a Greenpeace protest on Wednesday.

items.snippet: The U.S. Army is developing a program to deploy autonomous AI agents that can navigate digital and network infrastructures, identify targets, and “neutralize” them.

items.title: Remediation in the era of AI: Fix what matters first
items.snippet: Every IT and security team knows the feeling of opening a vulnerability report and seeing a number that only goes up. Thousands of findings. Hundreds marked critical. A backlog that grows faster than any team can close it. For years, the default response has been to work harder: more scans, more tickets, more overtime. But the volume of vulnerabilities , accelerated by AI-assisted discovery and a sprawling mix of endpoints, cloud services, and applications, has outpaced that approach. Shift from vulnerability counts to exposure reduction → The question has shifted from, “How do we fix everything?” To, “What should we fix first, and why?” Vulnerabilities are not the same as exposures A vulner

items.title: The Patch Apocalypse is here. Patching everything isn’t the answer.
items.snippet: For most IT teams, Patch Tuesday used to set the rhythm of the month. Updates arrived, teams tested them, change boards approved them, and deployments rolled out over the following weeks. It wasn’t painless, but it was predictable. That predictability is gone. Nearly 48,000 CVEs were published in 2025 , and the average time to exploit has collapsed to roughly five days. Attackers no longer wait for organizations to finish their testing cycles. Move from reactive patching to risk-based automation → Many practitioners now call this the Patch Apocalypse. The name is dramatic, but the operational reality behind it is not. It’s a capacity problem, prioritization problem, and process problem, all

items.title: Rogue AI: When agents stop advising and start acting
items.snippet: For the past few years, most enterprise AI has been advisory. It summarized tickets, drafted knowledge articles, and suggested next steps. A person still decided what to do. That’s changing. Agentic AI systems can plan multistep tasks and carry them out: querying systems, triggering workflows, changing configurations, and closing tickets with little or no human involvement. Ivanti’s 2026 State of Cybersecurity Report found that 87% of security professionals say integrating agentic AI is a priority, and 77% report at least some comfort letting autonomous systems act without human review. Secure every AI agent before its first action → The appeal is obvious for IT teams under constant pressure

items.title: AI isn’t hallucinating—but your data might be
items.snippet: “Hallucination” has become the catch-all term for AI getting things wrong. It describes a real phenomenon: Large language models can generate confident, fluent answers that are simply untrue. But in IT operations, many errors labeled as hallucinations have a more ordinary explanation. The AI isn’t inventing facts. It’s faithfully reporting information that happens to be outdated, incomplete, or contradictory. I’ve seen this play out across enough environments to know the cause usually sits upstream, in the data the system learned from and the picture of the estate it read. items.title: AI didn’t create your IT data problem, it just exposed it
items.snippet: When an AI pilot in IT operations underdelivers, the first instinct is to question the technology. Was the model wrong? Did the tool overpromise? Did the team pick the wrong use case? These certificates were widely trusted by browsers, operating systems, and also within Cloudflare. Because the keys themselves are weak, an attacker can create a forged certificate for any domain and use it to impersonate servers to intercept or modify traffic. This is a serious security incident with implications across the Internet. For reference, here is a link to more information about how SSL certificates work and why they are so critical to the operation of the Internet. We immediately prioritized patching critical services across Cloudflare to protect our customers ahead of the public disclosure of the vulnerability. Our security review has not identified active exploitation of this issue on Cloudflare services. items.title: Gartner’s top tech trends for 2027 expand—and constrain—AI capabilities
items.snippet: Gartner kicked off its IT Symposium/Xpo this week and unveiled its annual list of the top strategic technology trends that organizations need to explore in the coming year. items.title: AI agents drive up telemetry costs, complicate network observability
items.snippet: AI agents are driving up telemetry costs and complicating network management as enterprises struggle to monitor the technology and control unexpected expenses, according to new research from Cisco Splunk . The company’s State of Observability 2026 report found that 57% of organizations have observability costs that exceed the cost of the infrastructure being monitored. Another 60% said unexpected billing spikes create more operational strain than consistently high costs, and 55% cannot accurately control their AI expenses. Cisco Splunk surveyed 2,050 IT operations and engineering professionals across 10 countries to understand how AI agents are affecting observability practices and costs . “
